{{Short description|Countable intersection of open sets}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:G<sub>δ</sub> set}}
In [[general topology]], a '''G<sub>δ</sub> set''' is a [[subset]] of a [[topological space]] that is a [[countable]] [[Intersection (set theory)|intersection]] of [[open set]]s. The notation originated from the [[German language|German]] nouns {{wikt-lang|de|Gebiet}} {{gloss|open set}} and {{wikt-lang|de|Durchschnitt}} {{gloss|intersection}}.<ref name="ramtihs">{{cite book |last1= Stein |first1= Elias M. |author-link=Elias M. Stein |last2= Shakarchi |first2= Rami |date= 2009 |title= Real Analysis: Measure Theory, Integration, and Hilbert Spaces |publisher= [[Princeton University Press]] |isbn= 9781400835560 |page= 23 |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=2Sg3Vug65AsC&pg=PA23}}</ref>
Historically G<sub>δ</sub> sets were also called '''inner limiting sets''',<ref>{{cite book |last1= Young |first1= William |last2= Young |first2= Grace Chisholm |date= 1906 |title= Theory of Sets of Points |publisher= Cambridge University Press |author-link= William Henry Young |author-link2= Grace Chisholm Young |url= https://archive.org/stream/theoryofsetsofpo00youniala#page/n3/mode/2up |page= 63}}</ref> but that terminology is not in use anymore.
G<sub>δ</sub> sets, and their dual, [[Fσ set|F<sub>σ</sub> sets]], are the second level of the [[Borel hierarchy]].

==Definition==

In a topological space a '''G<sub>δ</sub> set''' is a [[countable]] [[intersection (set theory)|intersection]] of [[open set]]s. The G<sub>δ</sub> sets are exactly the level '''Π'''{{su|p=0|b=2}} sets of the [[Borel hierarchy]].

==Examples==

* Any open set is trivially a G<sub>δ</sub> set.
* The [[irrational numbers]] are a G<sub>δ</sub> set in the real numbers <math>\R</math>. They can be written as the countable intersection of the open sets <math>\{ q \}^{c}</math> (the superscript denoting the [[Complement (set theory)|complement]]) where <math>q</math> is [[Rational number|rational]].
* The set of rational numbers <math>\Q</math> is {{em|not}} a G<sub>δ</sub> set in <math>\R</math>.  If <math>\Q</math> were the intersection of open sets <math>A_n</math> each <math>A_n</math> would be [[Dense set|dense]] in <math>\R</math> because <math>\Q</math> is dense in <math>\R</math>.  However, the construction above gave the irrational numbers as a countable intersection of open dense subsets.  Taking the intersection of both of these sets gives the [[empty set]] as a countable intersection of open dense sets in <math>\R</math>, a violation of the [[Baire category theorem]].
* The [[Continuity set#Continuity set of a function|continuity set]] of any real valued function is a G<sub>δ</sub> subset of its domain (see the "Properties" section for a more general statement).
* The zero-set of a [[Derivative (mathematics)|derivative]] of an everywhere differentiable real-valued function on <math>\R</math> is a  G<sub>δ</sub> set; it can be a dense set with empty interior, as shown by [[Pompeiu derivative#Pompeiu's construction|Pompeiu's construction]].
* The set of functions in <math>C([0,1])</math> not differentiable at any point within {{closed-closed|0, 1}} contains a dense G<sub>δ</sub> subset of the metric space <math>C([0,1])</math>. (See {{section link|Weierstrass function|Density of nowhere-differentiable functions}}.)

==Properties==

The notion of G<sub>δ</sub> sets in [[Metric space|metric]] (and [[Topological space|topological]]) spaces is related to the notion of [[Complete metric space|completeness]] of the metric space as well as to the [[Baire category theorem]].  See the result about completely metrizable spaces in the list of properties below.  G<sub>δ</sub> sets and their complements are also of importance in [[real analysis]], especially [[measure theory]].

=== Basic properties ===
* The [[Complement (set theory)|complement]] of a G<sub>δ</sub> set is an [[Fσ set|F<sub>σ</sub>]] set, and vice versa.
* The intersection of countably many G<sub>δ</sub> sets is a G<sub>δ</sub> set.
* The union of {{em|finitely}} many G<sub>δ</sub> sets is a G<sub>δ</sub> set.
* A countable union of G<sub>δ</sub> sets (which would be called a G<sub>δσ</sub> set) is not a G<sub>δ</sub> set in general.  For example, the rational numbers <math>\Q</math> do not form a G<sub>δ</sub> set in <math>\R</math>.
* In a topological space, the [[zero set]] of every real valued continuous function <math>f</math> is a (closed) G<sub>δ</sub> set, since <math>f^{-1}(0)</math> is the intersection of the open sets <math>\{x \in X : -1/n < f(x) < 1/n\}</math>, <math>(n = 1, 2, \ldots)</math>.
* In a [[metrizable]] space, every [[closed set]] is a G<sub>δ</sub> set and, dually, every open set is an F<sub>σ</sub> set.<ref>Willard, 15C, p. 105</ref>  Indeed, a closed set <math>F \subseteq X</math> is the zero set of the continuous function <math>f(x) = d(x, F)</math>, where <math>d</math> indicates the [[Distance to a set|distance from a point to a set]].  The same holds in [[pseudometrizable]] spaces.
* In a [[first countable]] [[T1 space|T<sub>1</sub> space]], every [[Singleton (mathematics)|singleton]] is a G<sub>δ</sub> set.{{sfn|Engelking|1989|p=37}}
* A [[topological subspace|subspace]] of a [[completely metrizable]] space <math>X</math> is itself completely metrizable if and only if it is a G<sub>δ</sub> set in <math>X</math>.<ref>Willard, theorem 24.12, p. 179</ref><ref>Engelking, theorems 4.3.23 and 4.3.24 on p. 274.  From the historical notes on p. 276, the forward implication was shown in a special case by S. Mazurkiewicz and in the general case by M. Lavrentieff; the reverse implication was shown in a special case by P. Alexandroff and in the general case by F. Hausdorff.</ref>
* A subspace of a [[Polish space]] <math>X</math> is itself Polish if and only if it is a G<sub>δ</sub> set in <math>X</math>.  This follows from the previous result about completely metrizable subspaces and the fact that every subspace of a separable metric space is separable.
* A topological space <math>X</math> is Polish if and only if it is [[homeomorphic]] to a G<sub>δ</sub> subset of a [[Compact space|compact]] [[metric space]].<ref>Fremlin, p. 334</ref><ref>The sufficiency of the condition uses the fact that every compact metric space is separable and complete, and hence Polish.</ref>
* A topological space <math>X</math> is perfectly normal if and only if it is both normal and has each closed set of <math>X</math> being G<sub>δ.</sub><ref>Kelley, p.134</ref>

=== Continuity set of real valued functions ===

The set of points where a function <math>f</math> from a topological space to a metric space is [[Continuous function|continuous]] is a G<sub>δ</sub> set.  This is because continuity at a point <math>p</math> can be defined by a <math>\Pi^0_2</math> formula, namely: For all positive integers <math>n,</math> there is an open set <math>U</math> containing <math>p</math> such that <math>d(f(x), f(y)) < 1/n</math> for all <math>x, y</math> in <math>U</math>. If a value of <math>n</math> is fixed, the set of <math>p</math> for which there is such a corresponding open <math>U</math> is itself an open set (being a union of open sets), and the [[universal quantifier]] on <math>n</math> corresponds to the (countable) intersection of these sets.  As a consequence, while it is possible for the irrationals to be the set of continuity points of a function (see the [[popcorn function]]), it is impossible to construct a function that is continuous only on the rational numbers.

In the real line, the converse holds as well; for any G<sub>δ</sub> subset <math>A</math> of the real line, there is a function <math>f : \R \to \R</math> that is continuous exactly at the points in <math>A</math>.<ref>{{cite web |last1= Saito |first1= Shingo |title= Properties of G<sub>δ</sub> subsets of <math>\mathbb{R}</math> |url=http://www.artsci.kyushu-u.ac.jp/~ssaito/eng/maths/Gdelta.pdf}}</ref>

==G<sub>δ</sub> space==

A '''[[Gδ space|G<sub>δ</sub> space]]'''<ref>Steen & Seebach, p. 162</ref> is a topological space in which every [[closed set]] is a G<sub>δ</sub> set.{{sfn|Johnson|1970}} A [[normal space]] that is also a G<sub>δ</sub> space is called [[Perfectly normal space|perfectly normal]].  For example, every metrizable space is perfectly normal.

== See also ==

* [[Fσ set|F<sub>σ</sub> set]], the [[Duality (mathematics)|dual]] concept; contrast the "G" from [[German language|German]] {{wikt-lang|de|Gebiet}} {{gloss|open set}} and "F" from [[French language|French]] {{wikt-lang|fr|fermé}} {{gloss|closed}}.
* [[P-space|''P''-space]], any space having the property that every G<sub>δ</sub> set is open
